title: TaskFlow — Kanban Task Manager
problem: I wanted a full-stack board app I could take all the way to production standards rather than stopping at 'it works locally' — real authentication, real authorization on every write, tests, and a deployment pipeline.
architecture: NestJS REST API over MongoDB with a React + TypeScript front end. Authentication uses short-lived JWT access tokens with refresh-token rotation, and every mutation re-checks that the board, list, or card actually belongs to the requesting user rather than trusting the ID in the request. The app ships as multi-stage Docker builds, and a GitHub Actions pipeline runs the unit test suite on every push.
outcome: A board app with per-user data isolation enforced server-side, a unit-tested service layer, reproducible container builds, and CI that fails the build when tests break.
keyEngineering: JWT auth with refresh-token rotation, per-user ownership checks on every mutation, unit tests, multi-stage Docker builds, and a GitHub Actions pipeline.
lessons: Ownership checks belong on every mutation, not just at login — an authenticated user is not automatically an authorized one
Rotating refresh tokens limits the damage window if a token leaks, at the cost of a lookup on refresh
Multi-stage Docker builds keep the runtime image free of build-time dependencies
Wiring CI early meant the test suite stayed honest instead of rotting after the first red build

title: Simple Analytics API — Privacy-First Web Analytics
problem: Most drop-in analytics means handing visitor data to a third party. I wanted a page-view tracking service small enough to self-host, that answers the few questions that actually matter without profiling anyone.
architecture: A NestJS service running on the Fastify adapter over MongoDB. Incoming events pass through DTO validation at the boundary so malformed payloads are rejected before they reach the database, and aggregation endpoints return daily, referrer, and browser breakdowns. The whole API surface is documented with Swagger/OpenAPI.
outcome: A self-hostable analytics API with validated inputs, useful breakdowns, and browsable OpenAPI docs — no third-party analytics vendor in the request path.
keyEngineering: NestJS on Fastify with DTO validation at the boundary, aggregation by day/referrer/browser, and full Swagger/OpenAPI documentation.
lessons: Validating at the DTO boundary keeps malformed data out of the database instead of defending against it at every read
Chose the Fastify adapter over Express for an endpoint whose whole job is absorbing frequent, small writes
Generated OpenAPI docs make an API testable by anyone without reading the source first
Deciding what not to collect was as much a design decision as the schema itself

title: Vocab Bot — Vocabulary Learning Bot
problem: Typing vocabulary into a flashcard app by hand is the step where learning actually stops. I wanted to photograph a page of text and have the words become reviewable cards without any manual entry.
architecture: A Python Telegram bot where a photographed page is passed to a vision model that extracts the vocabulary into flashcards. Review scheduling uses the Leitner spaced-repetition system, backed by SQLite with a language-neutral schema so the bot is not tied to any particular language pair. The bot also generates audio tracks for cards and sends scheduled review reminders.
outcome: A working Telegram bot that turns a photo of a page into scheduled, audio-backed flashcards — removing the manual data entry that usually kills a vocabulary habit.
keyEngineering: Vision-model text extraction into flashcards, Leitner spaced repetition over a language-neutral SQLite schema, generated audio, and scheduled reminders.
lessons: Keeping the schema language-neutral meant a new language needed no migration
Leitner boxes gave most of the benefit of spaced repetition with far less complexity than an interval-scoring algorithm
Scheduled reminders turned out to matter more for retention than any feature inside the review flow
Vision extraction needs a human confirmation step — a wrong card is worse than a missing one
